title: Causative and causative receptive
summary: せる / させる makes someone or something do an action. Add られる and you get "was made to". Each verb in the chain has its own doer.

blocks.text: Both helpers attach to the **あ-stem**. The **receptive** れる / られる (lesson 13) is the close relative of ある ("be"), the mother of self-move verbs. The **causative** せる / させる is the relative of する ("do"), the father of other-move verbs. Textbooks call them conjugations, but a verb plus a helper is really **two verbs with two doers**.

Godan verbs take **せる**, ichidan verbs take **させる**: 飲む → 飲ませる, 食べる → 食べさせる. It means "to cause X to happen" by any means. "Make" and "let" are only partial translations: you may have forced it, allowed it, or simply arranged things so it happened.

The one who actually does the action (the **causee**) takes **を** or **に**. Using を treats them as an object, with no will of their own, which fits compulsion. Using に treats them as a target and suggests more cooperation. But when the attached verb already has its own を, the causee must take **に**, so there are not two を in the sentence.

blocks.jp: 母は子供に野菜を食べさせた。
blocks.en: The mother made her child eat vegetables.

blocks.text: Drop る from せる / させる and add **られる**. It is an ichidan helper, so you get 食べさせられる: "to receive being made to eat". A sentence like this has **three verbs and two doers**: the first and the last verb share the person who was forced, and the middle verb belongs to the person who forced them.
私はブロッコリーを食べさせられた。 I was made to eat broccoli.

blocks.jp: 私はブロッコリーを食べさせられた。
blocks.en: I was made to eat broccoli.

items: **あ-stem + せる** (godan), **させる** (ichidan): make / let / cause.
The causee takes **を** or **に**; if the verb has its own **を**, use **に**.
**させ + られる** = **させられる**: "was made to".
Think in separate verbs with separate doers.

questions.note: あ-stem 読ま + せる.
Ichidan verbs take させる.
Ichidan: drop る and add させる.
The teacher is the causer; the students do the reading.
questions.en: The teacher made the students read a book.

questions.prompt: 母は子供＿＿手を洗わせた。
questions.note: The verb already has を, so the causee takes に.
questions.en: Mother made the child wash his hands.

questions.note: With no other を in the sentence, the causee can take を.
questions.en: I made my little brother run.

questions.note: させ + られる = させられる.

questions.instruction: Fill the gap: "I was made to eat vegetables by my mother"
questions.note: I am the one who was forced: causative + receptive.
questions.en: I was made to eat vegetables by my mother.

questions.prompt: 先生は生徒に漢字を書かせた。
questions.note: The causee (に) does the action.
questions.en: The teacher had the students write kanji.

questions.prompt: 私は兄に掃除をさせられた。
questions.note: The first and last verb share the forced person.
questions.en: I was made to clean by my older brother.

questions.instruction: Tap the person who made someone do it
questions.note: The causer is the main carriage of the whole sentence.
questions.en: Mother made my little brother practice the piano.

questions.instruction: Tap the causee (the one who stands up)
questions.note: The causee takes を or に.
questions.en: The teacher made the student stand up.

questions.instruction: Tap the one who actually drinks
questions.note: The causee does the action.
questions.en: I made my little brother drink milk.

questions.note: Causee を + causative verb.

questions.prompt: Mother made me do my homework.
questions.note: The verb has its own を, so the causee takes に.
questions.en: Mother made me do my homework.

questions.prompt: I was made to eat fish by my father.
questions.note: Forced person は, causer に, causative receptive.
questions.en: I was made to eat fish by my father.

questions.prompt: The causee takes に when the attached verb already has を.
questions.note: This avoids two を in one sentence.

questions.prompt: A causative sentence always means the person was forced, never allowed.
questions.note: The causative means "cause it to happen": forcing, allowing or arranging.

questions.prompt: 子供に好きな本を読ませた。
options: The child let me read a book
I was made to read the book
I let the child read a book he likes
questions.note: Causative: the child reads; the speaker causes it.
questions.en: I let the child read a book he likes.

questions.instruction: 食べさせられた chains 食べる + させる + られる, and involves the person forced to eat and the person forcing. How many verbs and doers is that?
questions.note: 食べる + させる + られる, with the forced person and the forcer.

questions.instruction: Which one is NOT a causative?
questions.note: 食べられる is a receptive (or potential).

questions.instruction: In the course's terms, する is the "father" of the other-move verbs (verbs that act on something, like 出す). Which verb is せる / させる a relative of?
questions.note: The causative is the relative of する, the father of other-move verbs.
